rounds.proof_sketch: Block dimensions are dim3(32, 32), so threadIdx.y ∈ [0,31] and threadIdx.x ∈ [0,31]. A_tile is written via A_tile[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] and read via A_tile[threadIdx.y][k] where k ∈ [0,31]. All accesses use first index ≤ 31. Changing array size from [32][32] to [33][32] adds row index 32 which is never accessed. Memory layout for indices [0..31][0..31] remains identical (row-major with stride 32).
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the shared memory array A_tile from dimensions [32][32] to [33][32]. This only adds an extra row at index 32. Since the kernel uses 32×32 thread blocks, threadIdx.y is always in range [0,31]. All write operations use A_tile[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] and all read operations use A_tile[threadIdx.y][k] where k iterates from 0 to 31. Therefore, the extra row at index 32 is never written to or read from. The memory layout for the accessed portion [0..31][0..31] is identical in both versions (row-major with 32 elements per row). This is purely dead allocation that has no effect on computation.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable. The mutation only affects array size, not the memory layout or access patterns for indices that are actually used. No input values can trigger access to the extra row since thread indices are hardware-constrained by the block dimensions.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should recognize that increasing the first dimension of a multi-dimensional shared memory array without changing access patterns creates an equivalent mutant. A static analysis pass checking if the new array bounds exceed all possible index values would identify this as dead allocation.
